samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers spot that the confirmations are inverted relative to risk. Both propose undo or Trash in place of the routine dialogs, a specific confirmation for voiding an emailed invoice, and removing the 'Invoice deleted' modal. B is cleaner: it treats draft delete as cheap once it can be recovered, flags its assumptions explicitly (it declines to set a retention period) and gives a clear order of work. A's table calls draft delete 'destructive', it picks an arbitrary 30-day retention, and its steps 1 and 2 overlap a little. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers spot the core problem: routine actions get dialogs while voiding an emailed invoice gets none. Both propose undo, a specific void confirmation and removing the 'Invoice deleted' dialog. B explains more clearly why undo is faster (the dialog's cost is paid on every action, including the 99% that were correct), and its fix order is more explicit, but its steps 1 and 2 overlap. A wins on avoiding invented details: it declines to pick a Trash retention period, uses a [date] placeholder and flags its assumptions. B states a 30-day retention, a backend `deleted_at` flag and an empty working directory as if they were facts.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly spot that the confirmations are inverted: they guard cheap actions and leave the emailed-invoice void unguarded. Both propose undo and trash in place of the routine dialogs, and both write a specific void confirmation. A edges ahead with an explicit, dependency-aware fix order ('don't remove dialogs before undo works') and clearly flagged assumptions. B's caveats about reconciliation locks and whether a void can be reversed are valuable, but its fix order is looser and some usage claims go unflagged. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers spot the inverted confirmations, replace routine dialogs with undo, and propose a specific confirmation for voiding an invoice. B gives a clearer order of work and warns not to remove the dialogs before undo exists. Its void dialog also handles the real consequence, that the client still has the original, by offering to send a notice. A's example states as fact that the client is not notified automatically, which the request doesn't say, and B drifts slightly with the colour and screen-reader notes and the bulk-actions guess.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers spot the inverted safeguards and propose undo plus a specific confirmation for voiding the emailed invoice. B gives a clearer reason why the routine dialogs are harmful: people learn to click through them, so the one dialog that matters gets dismissed too. B also gives a cleaner fix order and flags uncertainty about reconcile. A wanders a little into bulk select and keyboard shortcuts, and states some unflagged specifics, such as voids being legal records and clients not being notified automatically. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers spot the inverted safeguards, put undo ahead of removing the dialogs, write a specific void confirmation and call the 'Invoice deleted' OK box useless. B is slightly stronger: it explains that the lack of recovery is why the dialogs exist, lists its assumptions up front, and adds sensible behavioral details such as a Trash with retention, save-failure states and screen-reader support. Its 'Later' section is still about behavior rather than styling, but it moves a little beyond the request.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers reject the single-pattern premise and give a specific confirmation for Send. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers cover the same core pattern: a checkbox column, a contextual bar with a count, and select-all scoped to the current filter. A is more consistent and more complete. It keeps hidden selections visible ('2 hidden by filters'), gives each action a clear treatment matched to its cost (undo for check-in and cancel, a preview before texting, a staged reschedule), and says plainly that the selection clears after an action except for failed rows. B contradicts itself on Send reminder, first calling it a single click with Undo and then saying it gets a confirm dialog. It is also vaguer about what happens to the rows after an action. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers use a sticky contextual action bar, scope select-all to the current filters, and include keyboard and range selection. B weighs the actions by consequence more consistently: check-in and cancel get Undo, and the text gets a preview that names recipients. A first calls reminders low-risk and then requires a confirm dialog. B is also clearer about what happens to the rows after an action: the selection clears and failed rows stay selected. B keeps hidden selections and shows how many are hidden, which is as defensible as A's rule of clearing them.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers use a checkbox column and an action bar that appears only when rows are selected, and both handle rows hidden by filters well. A matches each action to its cost more closely: check-in, reschedule and cancel can all be undone, and a text gets one specific confirmation. A also covers fast selection more fully (Shift+arrows, Cmd+A, Cmd+Enter) and explains why the selection persists after an action. B's strengths are a bar that stays pinned while scrolling and good handling of partial failures, but cancel has no undo and its keyboard support is thin. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers use a contextual bar with a visible count, explain how hidden selections behave when filters change, and weigh each action by its consequences. B goes further on speed: it adds Shift+arrows, Cmd+A and Cmd+Enter, and it explains why the selection should persist after check-in. It also offers 'Show' and 'Deselect hidden' for hidden selections and adds Undo to cancel. A's partial-failure handling is a nice touch, but B covers more of the rubric overall. B spends a little length on filter chips and empty states, which drift slightly off scope.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers handle the contextual sticky bar, eligibility counts and filter-aware select-all well. A is stronger on reversibility: it offers Undo for cancel and reschedule, not just a confirmation. A also covers keyboard selection more fully (arrows, Shift+arrows, Esc) and says exactly how the selection behaves after each action. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers use a sticky contextual action bar, per-action eligibility counts, and graded confirmations, and they are about equal on selection visibility and filter semantics. B is stronger on recovery: it gives Undo for cancel and reschedule, adds a 'reminded' marker and a clear consequence-based rationale, and covers keyboard selection fully (arrows, Shift+arrows, Esc). A's handling of cancel confirmation is a bit vague ('typed or deliberate'), and it suggests a 'consider' for selection persistence instead of committing to it.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B wins narrowly because it gives explicit time bands (under 1s, 1–10s, over 10s) plus an indicator delay, which answers 'loading is loading' most directly; A only mentions a quarter-second threshold and otherwise sorts by action. A is better on failure handling (a stated rule that failures stay visible, a persistent download link) and is shorter. B runs longer, and its 'why it's worth doing' section drifts toward a lecture. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers propose sensible treatments for each action, and both cover the export flow well. B handles failure after the screen has moved on more directly ('failures stay visible until the customer notices them', plus save and rename errors), keeps the downloaded file reachable after the toast is gone, and reads more like a collegial message with open questions. A gives clearer explicit time bands, but it is longer and more lecture-like, and it says less about recovering from failed optimistic updates.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both drafts make the same core case: fast actions update in place without blocking, and export gets its own non-blocking progress UI. B is more concrete on the cases that matter most. It explicitly reverts a failed optimistic rename, lets the user leave the editor during export, delays the indicator for quick exports, and uses a browser notification so the finished file is easy to find. A is solid but organizes its tiers less consistently, and it spends extra length explaining what's wrong before it gets to the fix. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B organizes its proposal around explicit duration bands (very short, ongoing, long) and suggests a duration-class status model, which directly answers the 'loading is loading' claim. A covers the same ground per action and adds good details like the 300–500ms delay, an export snapshot and optimistic revert, but it frames the advice less clearly around time. A is somewhat tighter, while B's extra sections push it toward lecture length.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers sort actions by how long they take and remove the blocking spinner from the fast actions. B does more with failures after the screen has moved on: a save failure stays visible until it's fixed, and a failed rename reverts with a note next to the field. B also keeps an 'Export ready' state after the toast so the file is easy to find, and it says the export reflects the design as it was when the customer clicked. B is longer and more of a case, though, while A is slightly tighter, which is why A scores higher on tone and length. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers use time bands and recommend inline, non-blocking feedback for fast actions. A goes further on export completion: it keeps a persistent 'Export ready' state in case the customer misses the toast. A also handles failures more fully, with a save failure that stays visible until resolved and a rename that reverts with a message next to the field. Both are long for a colleague message, and B is slightly tighter, but A's more complete coverage of completion and recovery gives it the edge.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A says outright that the spec is sound and names the decisions worth keeping; B goes straight to listing problems. Both make the same main fixes (multi-page conflict, missing states, merchant source, unready drafts on submit), and both reprint the whole spec. A adds extras like on-phone reading and a screen-reader note, and its multi-page Done button adds a small step. B keeps the no-save-step rule more cleanly but makes more minor edits (30 days, singular button text). | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers find the same real problems: item 1 conflicts with item 7, item 3 leaves out states, merchant isn't read from the photo, and item 6 doesn't say what happens to unready drafts. Both also reprint the whole spec, which hurts them on brevity. A's fixes stay smaller and keep the no-save-step rule for multi-page by having later photos join the first draft. B adds a Done button, which brings back a save step, and also adds things nobody asked for: on-device reading, a screen-reader announcement and a link to fix drafts. B does say up front that the spec is sound, and A does not.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Neither answer treats the spec as essentially sound: both rewrite it in full, and both add the same multi-page Done flow and handling for incomplete drafts at submit. A splits several items into sub-lists, but most of its edits fix real ambiguities: the missing Waiting for signal state, which state wins when several apply, and the 10-second undo window in item 5. B keeps the original layout and says items 1, 4 and the submit confirmation are fine, but it adds more scope: an Upload failed state, reading the merchant from the photo, markers on guessed values and an accessibility note. A wins narrowly. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Neither answer treats the spec as sound: both reprint the whole spec and add more than a few edits, though both keep the core decisions (no save step, undo instead of a delete confirmation, the specific submit confirmation). A keeps the original prose and structure, and most of its changes are fixes to real contradictions, but it also adds new behavior (an Upload failed state, markers on guessed values, an accessibility note). B rewrites more: it turns items into bullet lists, adds a state priority order, and makes the camera close after each single photo. That last change is new behavior and could slow down reps capturing several receipts in a row.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers keep the core decisions and both reprint the whole spec, which pads the reply. A makes fewer, tighter fixes: the state list, the multi-page save rule, and '30 days' instead of 'a month'. It leaves the open questions, such as what submit does with incomplete drafts, to the requester. B states outright that the spec is sound but then adds a lot: a failed-upload state with Retry, screen-reader announcements, cancelling uploads on delete, and new submit rules that only include Ready expenses. That goes well past a once-over. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers find real problems: item 1 conflicts with item 7, item 4 has a state that item 3 doesn't list, and item 6 doesn't cover incomplete drafts. Both also restate the whole spec, which pads the reply. A adds more on its own authority: a failed-upload state with Retry, screen-reader announcements, cancelling the upload on delete, and its own rule for incomplete drafts at submit. B makes fewer changes and hands the open questions back to the owner as decisions, although it adds on-device reading and a 'thumb reach' line.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers spot the same problems and both put forgiving search first with a clear reason. A goes further on each fix: it keeps the query in a header search box, adds a 'Results for … · 3 of 24' strip with prev/next and Esc back to the list, and makes the no-results page offer a way to clear filters. B is tighter and more careful about what it can't know, but its fixes for the part page and keeping the user's place are thinner. A labels its assumptions and gaps, though it does assert search as 'the biggest cause' without data, and its optional side-panel idea leans toward a layout redesign. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers cover the same problems and put forgiving search first, then keeping state on Back, with clear reasons. B gives more detail on the part-page context strip and the search box in the header, but it adds unprompted assumptions about how staff work, calls search the biggest cause of the clunky feeling without data, and floats a side-panel layout change.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers find the same six problems, put search matching first with a clear reason, fix the dead-end empty state, and stay on behavior rather than visual redesign. B is slightly better because it says outright that it hasn't seen usage data and explains how the zero-result query logs could move Back-button state loss to first place. A adds an unlabeled assumption that a customer is often waiting, and B's guess that search fails on 'a large share' of lookups is hedged speculation, so neither is perfect on item 5. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers find the same six problems and put search matching first, with a clear reason. B goes further on the user's lost place and context: it adds a '3 of 14' position, a header search box that keeps the current query, keyboard access and a checklist to verify the fixes. A's strong point is saying when to reorder the fixes (move the Back-button fix to first if zero-result logs show clean part names), but it also guesses at failure rates. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers find the same six problems. Both put search matching and a useful empty state first, with keeping state across Back second, and both end with header search, a breadcrumb and next/previous. A states its assumptions up front and notes that synonyms are a data task, but it asserts things it can't know, such as 'comparing parts is the main job' and 'next most frequent annoyance'. B is tighter, and its caveat says how the order should change if logs show few zero-result queries, but it also presents guesses as fact, such as model numbers being the most common query and staff comparing several parts per lookup. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers rank search matching first and losing your place on Back second, with similar fixes. B is better: it states its assumptions up front and says no usage data was given. Its empty-state design is more complete because it names the active filters and offers to clear them, and it links the header search, part-page context and next/previous into a clear order. A covers the same ground more briefly but states a guess as likely fact ('probably their most common query'); its strong point is a caveat saying when the priorities should flip.

B covers the fast path more concretely: one-key presets, remembered defaults shown with their assumptions, and keyboard-first entry that follows the order of the call. It also adds a named override, undo, and passive conflict badges. A is shorter and clear, but its fast-path details are thinner, while B is longer but still well organized.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers side mostly with the dispatchers, push the double-assignment fix to the server as an atomic check, and offer an optional guided mode for new hires. B gives more concrete detail on the fast path (tab order, remembered defaults, autofill, one-key templates) and the conflict flow (an inline message with a one-key reassign). It also points out that a confirmation wouldn't have stopped either incident. A is tighter and more readable, but its per-call time figures are invented, and its fast-entry advice is thinner. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers side with the dispatchers, fix double assignment with an atomic server-side check, live status updates and undo, and give new hires an optional guided mode. A covers the fast path in more detail: tab order, remembering the last choice and caller autofill. B is shorter and blunter, rough as its per-shift cost estimates are, and its warnings only when something looks wrong (truck busy, wrong equipment, too far away) are a sharper replacement for the blanket confirmation.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers side with the dispatchers and treat the double-assignment as a system problem to fix with atomic server-side assignment and live status. B goes further on keeping work fast (one-key templates, remembering the last choice, a keyboard-only flow) and offers undo plus a logged override at the moment of assignment. It also acknowledges the GM's goal more fully. A is a little tighter and adds a sensible database constraint, but its fast-path advice is thin. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers side with the dispatchers and treat the double-assignments as a problem to fix inside the system rather than with a dialog. A is more concrete about keeping entry fast: one-key templates, remembering the last value per field, and keyboard-only entry. It also handles conflicts at the point of assignment, with busy trucks shown greyed out alongside their current job, a logged override, and an undo after assigning.
